paper_metadata.title: Quantum Computing for Supply Chain Finance

summary: The paper studies trade-finance portfolio selection over 10 companies using 20 performance parameters and compares three methods: a classical Minimum Eigenvalue Algorithm, VQE, and QAOA. Across 6 selected companies and q values from 0.0 to 1.0, the classical method achieved the highest average accuracy (0.566667) versus VQE (0.446667) and QAOA (0.418333), with no statistically significant difference reported by ANOVA (F(2,15)=0.964958, p=0.403435).

experiments.description: Portfolio optimization for trade finance using a classical minimum-eigenvalue algorithm, VQE, and QAOA on 6 selected companies out of 10, evaluated across risk-aversion values q from 0.0 to 1.0 and compared against an underwriter's manual selections.

algorithm.variant: QAOA for mean-variance portfolio optimization (Qiskit tutorial-based)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Binary variable x_i indicates whether company i is selected (1) or not (0); the tutorial-based portfolio optimization formulation is adapted to trade finance selection.
problem_formulation.objective_function: min q * x^T Σ x - μ^T x, with equality constraint 1^T x = B enforced via penalty term (1^T x - B)^2; maximize return under risk constraint by minimizing the penalized objective.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Equality constraint mapped to a quadratic penalty term scaled by a parameter and subtracted from the objective; risk appetite controlled by q.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Hamiltonian corresponding to the penalized mean-variance objective; minimum-energy ground state corresponds to optimal selection.

problem_instance.description: Trade finance portfolio selection over 10 companies from two sectors, selecting 6 companies for financing.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: Performance parameters collected from annual reports, quarterly filings, manual underwriting sections, and country risk evaluation parameters; weighted and summed into a score in Excel; covariance computed in Python/NumPy; interest rate used as equivalent return.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Scores mapped to values between 0 and 100 and weighted by underwriter-defined importance; covariance matrix computed from company scoring metrics; financing interest rate loaded as return equivalent.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Selections compared against manual underwriter selections for q in [0.0,1.0] in steps of 0.1; accuracy score computed by counting matches; cumulative accuracy summarized across 6 runs/configurations; ANOVA performed across algorithms.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Data extracted from Excel into Python lists using Pandas; covariance computed with NumPy; weighted scoring in Microsoft Excel.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Accuracy scores computed by comparing algorithmic selections to manual underwriter selections; ANOVA used for statistical comparison.

speedup_claims.conditions: All experiments executed on IBM quantum simulators; paper reports no statistically significant difference between classical and quantum algorithms.
speedup_claims.caveats: No quantum advantage or asymptotic speedup is shown; the paper explicitly states there is no statistical advantage and no disadvantage for VQE/QAOA versus the classical baseline.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No advantage resources identified; paper uses 10 binary variables / 10 qubits in simulation only.
limiting_factors: Classical baseline has higher average accuracy (0.566667) than QAOA (0.418333)
No statistical advantage is reported (ANOVA p = 0.403435)
Problem size is small: 10 companies / 10 qubits

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states all experiments were executed on quantum simulators and no QPU device is named.

The paper reports no statistical advantage for quantum algorithms over the classical baseline; speedup order set to none_proven because no asymptotic speedup is characterized.
